source_text:
A WATCHMAN.
I pray the gods to quit me of my toils,
To close the watch I keep, this livelong year;
For as a watch-dog lying, not at rest,
Propped on one arm, upon the palace-roof
Of Atreus’ race, too long, too well I know
The starry conclave of the midnight sky,
Too well, the splendours of the firmament,
The lords of light, whose kingly aspect shows—
What time they set or climb the sky in turn—
The year’s divisions, bringing frost or fire.
modern_text: A WATCHMAN. I pray the gods to release me from this labor, to end the watch I have kept this whole long year. Lying like a watchdog with no real rest, propped on one arm upon the palace roof of the house of Atreus, too long and too well I have come to know the starry council of the midnight sky — too well, the splendors of the firmament, those royal lords of light whose movements, as they rise and set in turn, mark out the seasons of the year, bringing frost or fire.

source_text:
_At home there tarries like a lurking snake,
Biding its time, a wrath unreconciled,
A wily watcher, passionate to slake,
In blood, resentment for a murdered child._
modern_text: For at home, like a lurking snake, there waits a wrath unreconciled, biding its time — a cunning watcher, passionate to slake in blood its vengeance for a murdered child.

source_text:
For this, for this, I say there plots revenge
A coward lion, couching in the lair—
Guarding the gate against my master’s foot—
My master—mine—I bear the slave’s yoke now,
And he, the lord of ships, who trod down Troy,
Knows not the fawning treachery of tongue
Of this thing false and dog-like—how her speech
Glozes and sleeks her purpose, till she win
By ill fate’s favour the desired chance,
Moving like Atè to a secret end.
O aweless soul! the woman slays her lord—
Woman? what loathsome monster of the earth
Were fit comparison? The double snake—
Or Scylla, where she dwells, the seaman’s bane,
Girt round about with rocks? some hag of hell,
Raving a truceless curse upon her kin?
Hark—even now she cries exultingly
The vengeful cry that tells of battle turned—
How fain, forsooth, to greet her chief restored!
Nay then, believe me not: what skills belief
Or disbelief? Fate works its will—and thou
Wilt see and say in ruth, _Her tale was true._
modern_text: For this, for this, I tell you, plots revenge a coward lion couching in the lair — guarding the gate against my master's foot — my master — mine — for I bear the slave's yoke now. And he, the lord of ships who trod down Troy, knows not the fawning, dog-like treachery of this false thing's tongue — how her speech glozes and slicks her purpose smooth, until by ill fate's favor she wins the moment she desires, moving like Ate to a secret end. O fearless soul! The woman slays her lord — woman? What loathsome monster of the earth would be a fit comparison? The double snake — or Scylla, where she dwells, the seamen's bane, girt round about with rocks? Some hag of hell, raving a truceless curse upon her kin? Hark — even now she lifts the exultant cry of vengeance that proclaims a battle turned — how eager, forsooth, to greet her chief restored! No, then — believe me not: what skills it whether you believe or not? Fate works its will — and you will see and say in pity: "Her tale was true."

source_text:
APOLLO.
O monsters loathed of all, O scorn of gods,
He that hath bound may loose: a cure there is,
Yea, many a plan that can unbind the chain.
But when the thirsty dust sucks up man’s blood
Once shed in death, he shall arise no more.
No chant nor charm for this my Sire hath wrought.
All else there is, he moulds and shifts at will,
Not scant of strength nor breath, whate’er he do.
modern_text: APOLLO. O monsters loathed of all, O scorn of gods — he who has bound may loose: there is a cure for that, yes, many a plan that can unbind the chain. But when the thirsty dust has sucked up a man's blood once shed in death, he shall arise no more. No chant or charm has my Sire wrought for this. All else there is, he molds and shifts at will, not scant of strength or breath, whatever he do.
